title: What is The continuum hypothesis and the sizes of infinite sets, marked off from everything adjacent to it — what space is this essay, and what is it NOT?
text: The continuum hypothesis posits that the set of real numbers has a cardinality greater than the set of integers, yet this assumption fundamentally misunderstands the nature of infinite sets.

title: Admission — Does The continuum hypothesis and the sizes of infinite sets name ONE
text:
[refused] Does The continuum hypothesis and the sizes of infinite sets name ONE being that clears its ground, or several that must be kept apart?
[matter] The continuum hypothesis, as initially conceived by Georg Cantor, challenges the notion of a single, definitive "being" that encapsulates all infinite sets.
[refused] Cantor's work laid the groundwork for the idea of infinite sets and their cardinality, but it also led to a fundamental problem: how to define and prove the existence of a set with cardinality between integers and real numbers.
[refused] This is where the generalized continuum hypothesis (GCH) attempts to address this issue.
[refused] GCH proposes that the cardinality of an infinite set falls between the cardinality of an infinite set S and the cardinality of its power set P(S).
[refused] If this condition is met, the set's cardinality would be equivalent to either S or P(S).
[refused] However, the GCH has not gained widespread acceptance within the mathematical community.
[refused] The continuum hypothesis itself has been the subject of extensive study and debate for years.
[refused] Kurt Gödel proved that the negation of the continuum hypothesis—the existence of a set with intermediate cardinality— could not be proven within standard set theory.
[refused] Paul Cohen's work in 1963 further solidified the independence of the continuum hypothesis.
[refused] The proof for this independence was a significant step in understanding the limitations of set theory and the nature of infinity itself.
